Week 8: Midterm Exam

sections.content:
Prof. YAN said that he made changes to lecture notes of MATH 2131 based on MATH 2121 he taught in Spring 2024. If you compare the contents with last year's MATH 2131 (which is taught by Ivan), the contents are relatively easy.

First 3 chapters are three different viewpoints of basic linear algebra, which is solving system of linear equations, vectors and linear transformations. These part are typically MATH 2121 stuff and are really easy.

Next in chapter 4 Prof. YAN talked about general real vector spaces (not Euclidean space) and makes conclusion on the first three chapters.
(Midterm exam)
He also discussed quotient space and dual space, which I found difficult to understand.

Chapter 5 skipped (about vector space over general field).

Chapter 6 is about orthogonality, orthogonal projection, orthogonal basis, G-S process, general inner product space.

Chapter 7 is about multi-linear map. In particular, determinant is an example of bilinear map. Focus on the properties of determinant.

Chapter 8 eigenvalue, eigenvector, eigenspace, diagonalization, normal operator, unitary opertor (both real and complex).

The only thing I want to complain is his lecture notes is difficult to read. Black words with white background and small font makes me tired. Also, he uses too many different notation which really confuse me a lot.

For detail, you may see the lecture notes this year.

sections.content:
The content is quite packed and is focused 100% on the concepts. That is to say that we barely do computation in this class, even when Ivan is doing worksheets he skips the computation or when there's computation in tutorials, no one really does it. So if you are not looking to go towards maths/science, I think you should instead take 2121 to get the necessary practice.
Also to note that while the title includes "abstract algebra", we really only touch some definitions like fields and rings in the first chapter and never again. While the general feel of "vectors can be anything" is always there, abstract algebra starts from 3131.
----------------------------------------------
Chapter 1: Abstract vector spaces
Chapter 2: Linear Transformation and Matrices
Chapter 3: Determinants
Chapter 4: Inner product spaces (mid term)
Chapter 5: Spectral theory (I LOVE THIS)
Chapter 6: PSD and SVD
Chapter 7: Complex matrices (I HATE THIS)
Chapter 8: Invariant subspaces
Chapter 9: Canonical forms (JCF and RCF)
Chapter 10: Quotient spaces and Dual spaces (not tested in final)

I love Ivan :))))))
His teaching is very clear: he goes step by step when he is explaining and never makes a mess of it, which is surprising because the proofs can get sophisticated in ch9 and 10 (although according to him everything is 1 liner :p ). He teaches for about 40 minutes, then gives 10 minutes break, then teaching for 40 minutes again. So you can always go to him in that break to clear something up. Although I will say, towards the end of the course when I sometimes got lost, I couldnt understand Ivan's reply to my questions (everything is too trivial to him orz). But I do think that is because I became too disconnected with the content that I needed to go through it properly on my own.
His lectures notes are a good summary of his lectures. Although if you want more practice or explainantion you really should look at other sources.
Tutorials for me fluctuated. Some times they were nice, some times they weren't. Tutorials are usually about some nice consequences of something taught in class or just revision (Lord Jiayi if you're reading this, you did an awsome job please do not reduce my grade).

sections.content:
*implodes*

Ivan teaches in this course:
- Vector spaces and inner products, the only abstract thing in this course. go to MATH 3131 if you want more. :)
- Matrices. Predominantly real or complex.
- Singular-value decomposition* and least-square approximation.
- Spectral theory (i.e. eigenxxxxx), diagonalization and Cayley-Hamilton theorem.
- Jordan canonical form* and rational canonical form*.
- Quotient spaces** and dual spaces**.
*: These content were not in Yan Min's MATH 2131.
**: These content were in both MATH 2131, but was not tested in examinations.

Or, for a less intimidating description:
    Once upon a time, there were sets. Elements of those sets, called vectors, can be added together or scaled, and the result is another element of the set.
    Now, there were special functions between two of those sets (possibly the same). Ivan said "the plusses and scalars shall be taken out of the arguments of these special functions", and the plusses and scalars were taken out of the arguments f(cu+v) = cf(u)+f(v), and Ivan said it was good.
    And apparently for each (finite dimensional) set there existed a very small subset of vectors that forms something completely describing the whole set, and then there were matrices (grid of numbers) which can represent any of those special functions (between finite dimensions). And MATH 2131 thus came to be.

Real life problems are hard.

sections.content:
Basically, content of the course was about basics of linear algebra, but compared to usual 2111 linear algebra course, it delves into concepts and ideas rather than just facts and their applications. If you like math, you'll especially find proofs of some theorems rather interesting. Here's all chapter that we've learnt (all are in lecture note written by the prof.):
1. Chapters before midterms
1)Vector space:
Just the basics and definitions of an abstract concept: takes some time to understand, though easy.
2)Linear transformation:
Just a bunch of definitions to understand, but one might like concept where linear transformations and matrices are quite related: by that idea it is very easy to deduce some algebraic facts with matrices (associativity,etc.). But part with dual spaces was kind of confusing because of professor's poor notations (I mean, really, he used "star" notation twice for two different things the book without clearly mentioning that they're,in fact different).
3)Subspace: 3.1 - Definition and 3.2 - Range and Kernel
Nice and easy chapter.
2. Chapter after midterms:
1)Subspace: 3.3 - Sum and Direct Sum and 3.4 - Quotient Space
3.3 is not that hard and 3.4 even wasn't include in final exam content.
2)Inner product
By far one of the most interesting chapter where I didn't force myself to read lecture notes.
3)Determinant
Here we covered concept of determinants in geometry and algebra.
4)General linear algebra - fields, complex vector space
Even though this chapter wasn't tested in final exam, this was the most interesting chapter to read and to work through.
SPOILER: you're going to prove that one cannot trisect angle with
a compass and a ruler.
5)Spectral Theory - eigenspaces/values
This chapter basically covers the idea of how to express linear transformation in a "good" and "convenient" form for some particular cases.
Yeah, it is the hardest and the most important theme in the final exam, so I suggest you to pay more attention to this chapter.

As a person who likes math, I'd say that in terms of coolness the content is bad. It's basically memorisation and understanding easy ideas (mostly).
sections.teaching:
Professor Yan Min is a very clever man, but I'd say his teaching skills are poor.  He likes to emphasise on unnecessary and usually obvious things and ignore important ones. Mostly even after his lecture you'll spend some time rereading previous chapters because you simply didn't understand him. Also, both his lectures and lectures note's structure is very loosely related to each other which makes it impossible to "absorb" the content. That is, you might get , say lecture 13, but after lecture 14 you'll just forget it. Fortunately, he's a very pleasant person to talk to and his english is decent.
Hopefully, his TAs (at least mine) were very nice and helpful. They always replied to your e-mails in 5-10 minutes at most and made pdf (in LATEX) solutions to problems by themselves. Combining TAs and professor, overall score would be C.
sections.grading:
Grading consists of:
20% - HW, 30% - midterms, 50% - finals

I used to hear by others that "grading is fair" and stuff, but it is not quite like that. I've got 93.74% and my final grade was A-
It is OK, but cut for A was 94% and for A+ was 98%. So you might see that classes are very competitive because all students have some background and most importantly "love" for math. I mean, most students are ready to spend 20-25 hours of their time to this course doing all HWs, so take this course if you really want this kind of pain.
Homework is totally another story. By the end of one chapter cycle (not necesserally end of one chapter), he gives 15-20 simple tasks. They're easy, but OMG it is so time consuming. I would love if there was 5-6 problems that are hard and time consuming, but it is so boring to solve lots of basic problems.
Midterms and finals are just 4-5 problems with themes covered (see content). He'll later send you sample papers, so don't worry about practicing. If you understand everything, it is not that hard to get high score.
I've got only final exam's electronic version, so sorry about that.
sections.workload:
Workload of this course is insane. Even if you don't have problems with planning and don't procrastinate, you'll spend 20-30 hours solely on this course (with some exceptions)!
I thought that the course is hard and interesting (im ok if i have to spend lots of time on it), but it turned out to be easy and boring, so regardless of if you like math or not, I wouldn't recommend to take it.
The only rational reason I can think of is nice suit for your transcript (some people will be "impressed" that you took "honors" course) or opportunity for scholarships (there are some scholarships with honors courses in math).
